newsitem.title: USA: Dollar closes in on eight-year highs vs German mark.
newsitem.headline: Dollar closes in on eight-year highs vs German mark.

text.p: The dollar, still rising on recent signals of a robust U.S. economy, surged to a near eight-year high vs the mark on Monday before concerns of rising German interest rates gave the market reason to pause.

The dollar hit an intraday high of 1.8730 marks before dipping back to 1.8675 marks at mid-afternoon in New York. The early rise sent the dollar to the highest level since it peaked at 1.9221 marks in October 1989.

It also registered a four-year high vs the Swiss franc, an eight-year peak vs the French franc and a near 12-year high vs the Italian lira. It was little changed vs the Japanese yen as that exchange rate continued to be hurt by fears of verbal intervention much beyond its current level of 118.23 yen.

Dealers said undeniable economic strength found in the U.S. employment and purchasing manager's reports on Friday encouraged investors to buy dollars vs the mark, which has come under heavy selling pressure amid widespread expectations that Europe's planned single currency, the euro, will be a weak one.

The U.S. Labour Department on Friday said U.S. businesses added 316,000 jobs to their payrolls in July, far more than analysts' average forecast for a gain of 193,000. The rise sent the jobless rate down to a 24-year low at 4.8 percent.
The report was complimented by the National Association of Purchasing Management's index of manufacturing activity, which jumped to a 2-1/2 year high to 58.6 in July from 55.7.
Furthermore, concerns that the German central bank will raise its short-term interest rates have dwindled.
"The Bundesbank has made practically no attempt whatsoever to stop (the mark's depreciation,) said Ben Strauss, assistant vice president with Bank Julius Baer.

"Then (Treasury Secretary Robert) Rubin put his stamp of approval on it last week saying he still wants a strong dollar because it helps control inflation and very quietly everybody is more of the opinion that the Germans see no way out of their dilemma."

At the same time, dealers exercised some degree of caution on Monday based on talk that the Bundesbank could open the door for higher interest rates as early as Tuesday. Though unlikely, the Bundesbank could add a second and variable official money market rate to its current fixed rate on Tuesday.

But the stagnant German economy has prompted traders to discount the likelihood of a rate rise. A stronger mark would make German exports more expensive, thereby suppressing potential economic growth, they said.

Traders were keenly watching for German employment data, due on Wednesday, for reinforcement of the recent dollar rally. A Reuters poll showed that economists expect a jobless rise of 4,000 and an unemployment rate of 11.3 percent.
The dollar edged down to 118.23 yen from 118.39 yen late Friday.
The pound fell to $1.6270 from $1.6305. The dollar rose to 1.5285 Swiss francs from 1.5265 and slid to Canadian $1.3790 from C$1.3812.
